raw_findings.message: Valid aliases are truncated to seven characters, so distinct aliases sharing the first seven characters resolve to the same code and can overwrite each other.
This stores expiration times in milliseconds, but `isExpired` compares them with seconds from `nowSeconds`, so links with TTLs remain usable long past their expiration.
Generated codes are inserted without checking for an existing entry, so a random collision overwrites the earlier link and breaks its short URL.
For links younger than one full day, `days` is zero and the resulting `NaN` or infinity is serialized as `null` instead of a numeric clicks-per-day value.
A stats request for an unknown code casts `undefined` to `Link` and dereferences it, causing a 500 response instead of handling the missing link.
The admin token is hardcoded in the source, so anyone who can inspect the project can send it in `X-Admin` and delete links.
When a caller requests a preview, this fetches their supplied URL and follows redirects without restricting destinations, allowing requests to internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints.
The preview reads the entire remote response into memory with no size limit, so a caller can exhaust server memory by requesting a preview of a very large response.
Concurrent redirects can read the same click count before either append completes and then both write the same incremented value, causing clicks to be undercounted.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Any positive integer TTL is accepted, including values beyond JavaScript's valid date range, which makes `linkStats` throw when it converts the resulting expiry timestamp to ISO format.
A link remains live when `now` equals `expiresAt` because expiration uses a strict less-than comparison, so a TTL link can still redirect at its stated expiration time.
The hostname is checked using a separate DNS lookup from the one `fetch` performs, so an attacker-controlled DNS record can resolve publicly during validation and to a private address when fetched.
Preview reads the entire remote response into memory before taking a 200-character snippet, so a target that streams a large response can exhaust server memory.
A supplied non-number `ttlSeconds` is silently converted to `undefined`, creating a link that never expires instead of rejecting the invalid TTL.
Deletion looks up the code without lowercasing it, so an uppercase spelling of a valid case-insensitive code fails to delete the link even though redirect and stats lookups accept it.

raw_findings.message: Aliases up to 8 characters are accepted but silently truncated to 7, so distinct valid aliases such as `abcdefgh` and `abcdefgi` resolve to the same code.
`expiresAt` is stored in milliseconds, but `isExpired` compares it with seconds from `nowSeconds()`, so links with positive TTLs do not expire.
This unconditionally replaces any existing link with the same code, allowing a chosen alias—or a generated-code collision—to hijack an existing short URL.
Aliases are stored in lowercase but looked up without normalization, so an alias created as `Example` cannot be resolved using `/r/Example` despite the case-insensitive alias contract.
For links less than one full day old, `days` is zero and the computed clicks-per-day value is `NaN` or infinite, which is serialized as `null` instead of a number.
An unknown code produces `undefined` here and causes a TypeError while building stats, so requesting stats for a nonexistent link returns a 500 instead of a not-found response.
The admin token is a fixed credential embedded in the source, so anyone who can obtain the code can authenticate to the delete endpoint.
When preview is requested, the user-controlled target is fetched directly, allowing requests to localhost, private-network services, or cloud metadata endpoints.
The entire remote response is read into memory without a size limit, so a preview target that returns a very large body can exhaust server memory.
Concurrent redirects can read the same click count before awaiting the log write and then both store the same incremented value, causing logged clicks to be missing from statistics.

fixed_raw_findings.message: `Number.isInteger` accepts integers too large for a valid JavaScript `Date`, so a link created with a sufficiently large TTL later causes its stats endpoint to throw while formatting the expiration.
A link remains resolvable when `now` equals `expiresAt` because expiration uses `<`, so links are still valid at their stated expiration time.

The hostname is checked with a DNS lookup before `fetch` resolves it again, so an attacker-controlled hostname can return a public address during validation and a private or loopback address during the fetch.
Preview responses are read fully into memory without a size limit, so repeated previews of large responses can exhaust the server's memory.
A supplied nonnumeric `ttlSeconds` value is converted to `undefined` instead of rejected, causing the link to be created without an expiration.
Deletion uses the submitted code without lowercasing it, so an uppercase spelling of a case-insensitive alias fails to delete the stored link.

raw_findings.message: Aliases are allowed to be eight characters but are truncated to seven here, so distinct aliases sharing their first seven characters resolve to the same code.
Expiration is stored in milliseconds, but `resolveLink` passes seconds to `isExpired`, so links with positive TTLs do not expire at their intended time.
A supplied TTL of zero is treated as if no TTL were supplied, making the link never expire instead of expiring immediately.
Setting an existing code unconditionally replaces its link, so creating a link with a duplicate alias—or randomly colliding generated code—silently changes the existing destination.
For links younger than one full day, `days` is zero, so the click rate becomes `NaN` or infinity and is serialized as `null` instead of a number.
An unknown stats code produces `undefined` here and is dereferenced below, causing the request to fail with a 500 instead of returning a not-found response.
The admin credential is fixed in source, so anyone who can inspect the application can authenticate to the delete endpoint.
When preview is requested, a user-controlled target is fetched without restricting hosts, allowing requests to loopback, private-network, or metadata services.
The entire preview response is buffered as text without a size limit, so a target serving a large response can exhaust server memory.
Concurrent redirects can read the same click count before the asynchronous log write and both store the same incremented value, undercounting clicks.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The positive-integer check accepts TTLs too large for JavaScript dates, allowing link creation to succeed but causing stats requests to throw when converting the expiry to an ISO date.
A link remains live when `now` equals `expiresAt`, so it can be used for an extra second after its configured TTL has elapsed.

The hostname is checked using one DNS lookup, but `fetch` resolves it again, so an attacker-controlled hostname can resolve publicly during validation and to a private address when the preview request is made.
`res.text()` buffers the entire preview response without a size limit, so a preview URL serving a large or fast-streaming body can exhaust server memory.
A supplied non-number `ttlSeconds` is converted to `undefined`, silently creating a non-expiring link instead of rejecting the invalid value.
Deletion uses the supplied code without lowercasing it, so an uppercase spelling of a valid case-insensitive link code cannot delete that link.
